A2.text:
Murad does not like art. But his girlfriend, Lala, loves it. On Sunday, she took him to a new exhibition at a gallery in Baku.

There were many abstract paintings. Murad looked at a big canvas with red and black lines. “A child can paint this,” he whispered.

Lala laughed. “Art is in the eye of the beholder,” she said. “Everybody sees something different. Good art can inspire you.”

They saw a big sculpture of a horse made from old car parts. Then a guide told them a story. “Last year, a famous painting came to this gallery. But it was a forgery! A clever man copied it.”

Murad liked that story, but he still did not like the art.

In the last room, there was one small painting. It showed an old woman at a window, waiting. Her face was sad, but her eyes were full of hope. Murad stopped. He looked at it for a long time.

“This one is a masterpiece,” he said quietly. “It is worth a thousand words. The colours paint a picture of her whole life.”

Lala smiled. “Who painted it?” Murad asked. There was no name.

“My grandmother,” Lala said. “She painted it when my grandfather was in the army. The gallery asked to show it.”

Murad was quiet. Then he said, “Can we come back next Sunday? I want to see more.”

A forgery is found in the gallery

B1.text:
Murad's idea of a perfect Sunday was football and a long lunch. Lala's was a gallery. So when she bought two tickets to a new exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art, he went the way a cat goes to the vet.

The first room was full of abstract work. Murad stood in front of a huge canvas covered in angry red lines and whispered, “My five-year-old nephew could paint that.”

“Beauty is in the eye of the beholder,” Lala whispered back. “You don't have to like it. Just ask yourself what it makes you feel.”

“Hungry,” said Murad.

In the second room, there was a sculpture of a running horse made entirely from old car parts, which he admitted was “quite cool”. A guide was telling a group about a famous forgery: a painting the museum had nearly bought ten years ago, until an expert noticed the paint was too modern. Murad listened to every word. That, at least, was a good story.

The last room was small and quiet. On the far wall hung a single painting with no name beside it. It showed an elderly woman sitting at a kitchen window, looking out at an empty street. Her hands were folded, her face was tired, but her eyes were bright with hope.

Murad stopped. He didn't speak for a long time.

“This one,” he said finally. “I don't know why, but this is a masterpiece. It's worth a thousand words. You can see she's waiting for someone she loves.”

Lala's eyes filled with tears. “My grandmother painted that,” she said. “In 1988, while my grandfather was working on the oil platforms for six months. The curator saw it at our house and asked to show it.”

Murad looked at the painting again, then at Lala. He had always thought art was something that happened to other people.

“Next Sunday,” he said slowly, “can we come back? I want to look at the others again. Properly this time.”

B2.text:
Murad's ideal Sunday involved football, a long lunch and, if possible, a nap. Lala's involved a gallery. So when she produced two tickets to a new exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art, he accompanied her with the enthusiasm of a cat being carried to the vet.

The first room was devoted to abstract work. Murad halted before a vast canvas slashed with furious red strokes and muttered, “My five-year-old nephew could knock that out before breakfast.”

“Beauty is in the eye of the beholder,” Lala murmured. “Nobody's asking you to love it. Just notice what it makes you feel.”

“Hungry,” Murad replied.

The second room held a sculpture of a galloping horse assembled entirely from scrap car parts, which he grudgingly conceded was “actually quite cool”. Nearby, a guide was entertaining a group with the tale of a notorious forgery — a canvas the museum had very nearly bought a decade earlier, until an expert spotted a pigment that hadn't existed in the artist's lifetime. Murad hung on every word. That, at least, was a proper story.

The final room was small and hushed. On the far wall hung a solitary painting with no label. It depicted an elderly woman seated at a kitchen window, gazing down an empty street. Her hands were folded in her lap and her face was worn with fatigue, yet her eyes held an almost unbearable brightness — the brightness of someone who refuses to stop hoping.

Murad stopped. For a long while he said nothing at all.

“This one,” he said at last. “I can't explain it, but this is a masterpiece. They say a picture is worth a thousand words — this one's worth a whole novel. She's waiting for someone she loves, and she's been waiting a long time.”

Lala's eyes brimmed. “My grandmother painted it,” she said. “In 1988, when my grandfather spent six months on the oil platforms. The curator saw it on our wall and begged to include it.”

Murad looked at the painting again, and then at Lala. He had always assumed that art was something that happened to other people.

“Next Sunday,” he said slowly, “could we come back? I'd like to look at the others again. Properly, this time.”

podcast.title: A red line on white

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Do you like modern art? Guess: what painting did Sam not understand?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is art and museums. And on Saturday I finally went to the Carpet Museum.
The building that looks like a rolled carpet! What did you think?
Amazing. Some of those carpets are real masterpieces. Three hundred years old!
And then?
Then the Museum of Modern Art. And honestly, I didn't understand everything.
[laugh] Abstract art?
There was one huge canvas — just a red line on white. People stood in front of it for ten minutes.
Maybe it made them feel something. Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
Maybe. But Aysu could paint that red line. [chuckle]
Funny you say that. Aysu had her first exhibition last week — at school.
A real exhibition?
In the school hall. Twenty children, two drawings each. She drew our grandmother in her garden.
I'd love to see it.
I'll send you a photo. When I saw it, I almost cried. A picture is worth a thousand words.
Do you have a favourite place for art in Baku?
A small gallery in the Old City. The artists are often there, and you can talk to them.
That's nice. In England I loved the sculpture parks — art in the open air, with trees all around.
Art doesn't have to be in a building. It can inspire you anywhere.
Even a red line on white. Okay — I'll go back and look again.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what kind of art do you like — and which museum would you love to visit?
And would you hang a red line on your wall? See you next time!
Bye for now!
